June 15, 2026 
 
 
The Honorable Mehmet Oz, M.D.  
Administrator  
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
Hubert H. Humphrey Building 
200 Independence Avenue, S.W. 
Room 445-G 
Washington, DC 20201 
 
 
Re: Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability 
Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid 
Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) 
Agencies and CHIP Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-
Facilitated Exchanges (CMS-0062-P) 
 
Dear Administrator Oz, 
 
On behalf of our more than 150 member hospitals and health systems, the Louisiana Hospital Association 
(LHA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS) 
proposal to extend its prior authorization (PA) interoperability framework to cover drugs. The LHA 
commends CMS for taking action to remove inappropriate barriers to patient care by streamlining the drug 
PA processes for the affected health plans and providers. The LHA supports extending many of the 
current interoperability requirements to drugs and adding small group market insurers participating in the 
Affordable Care Act small business exchange as organizations subject to the interoperability 
requirements. Providers benefit from standardization of processes across various payers. Currently, 
differing protocols depending on a patient’s insurance plan require multiple workflows to complete the 
same process thereby increasing administrative costs and contributing to provider burnout. 
 
While PA can be a tool to help ensure patients receive coverage for their care, the practice too often is 
used in a manner that leads to dangerous delays in treatment, clinician burnout, and waste in the 
healthcare system. The LHA supports efforts to reform PA processes across impacted payers and to 
reduce the significant administrative burden these practices impose on hospitals, clinicians, and patients. 
PA requirements for prescription drugs, particularly specialty and high-cost medications, frequently result 
in care delays, treatment interruptions, and substantial clinician and staff burden.  
 
Expansion of Electronic Prior Authorization Standards to Drugs 
PA is widely used by health plans as a utilization management tool, including for prescription drugs. While 
intended to promote appropriate care, PA is often applied in ways that delay treatment, increase costs, 
and divert clinical resources away from patient care. One of the most frustrating aspects of PA for 
providers is the variation in submission processes. Plans vary widely on accepted methods of PA requests  
 
 
 
and supporting documentation submission. For each plan, providers and their staff must ensure they are 
following the correct rules and processes, which may change from one request to the next. Moreover, the 
processes and standards for the PA of drugs often differ from that of medical items and services. 
Inevitably, providers commit inadvertent errors that result in denials that must be reprocessed or 
appealed. The expansion of standardized electronic PA transactions for drugs has the potential to save 
patients, providers, and utilization review entities considerable time and resources and can speed up the 
care delivery process.  
 
Currently, the Coverage Requirements Discovery Implementation Guide (IG) supports the Medication 
Request resource, and the Prior Authorization Support IG value set contains Healthcare Common 
Procedure Coding System J-codes used by providers for physician-administered drugs. Therefore, plans 
implementing the proposal already have the functionality needed to address drugs covered under the 
medical benefit. The proposed rule will close a loophole that these drugs currently fall through, improve 
communication and transparency, provide patients with continuity of care protections, and advance 
process efficiencies. We applaud CMS for taking these important steps to require plans to implement 
these critical PA and electronic data exchange reforms. 
 
Expansion of Impacted Payers 
The LHA applauds CMS’ proposal to require Medicare Advantage plans; Medicaid and Children’s Health 
Insurance Program (CHIP), both fee-for-service and managed care; and Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) 
on the Federally-facilitated Exchange — including small group QHPs offering plans on the Federally-
facilitated Small Business Health Options Program — to support electronic PA for prescription drugs. As 
CMS indicates, providers benefit from standardization of processes across various payers. Currently, 
differing protocols dependent on a patient’s insurance plan require the implementation of multiple 
workflows for completing the same process, thereby increasing administrative costs, and contributing to 
provider burnout. Hence, including these plans will significantly increase the volume of impacted patients 
and further encourage provider adoption and implementation.  
 
Standardized Drug Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes 
The LHA supports shorter PA decision times for drugs. Unlike many other transactions between providers 
and health plans, PA directly affects patient care and often stands between a patient and the start of 
treatment. For that reason, timely processing is essential. We appreciate that these timeliness standards 
would also apply to QHP issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges, and we believe patients enrolled 
in those plans deserve the same protections as others covered by this rule. Under the proposal, state 
Medicaid fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, and CHIP managed care entities would 
have 24 hours to decide requests for prescription drugs that are already subject to outpatient drug PA 
requirements. QHP issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchange would have 72 hours for standard 
requests and 24 hours for expedited requests. When non-drug items and services require PA, QHP 
issuers would follow the PA timeframes finalized in 2024 for items and services: 7 calendar days for 
standard requests and 72 hours for expedited requests. The proposed timeframes remain too lenient. 
When providers use the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) based transactions required 
by this rule, their electronic health record systems should supply the information needed to support prompt 
PA review. Likewise, health plans receiving clinical information electronically should be able to determine 
medical necessity more quickly. We therefore recommend that CMS apply the same timeframes proposed 
for drugs covered under a medical benefit across all medical services, requiring responses within 72 hours 
for standard, non-urgent requests, and 24 hours for urgent requests when the transaction uses the FHIR 
technology established under this rule. 
 
Adoption of Updated Interoperability Standards and Specifications 
Hospitals and health systems are eager to adopt and use technology that improves the safety, quality, and 
efficiency of care. In instances where adoption is slower, it is due to excessive financial cost or workforce 
burden that cannot be borne by the provider at that time. Under its HIPAA administrative simplification 
authority, the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services proposes to adopt certain HL7 FHIR 
 
standards and implementation specifications for electronic PA transactions related to drugs, including 
eligibility checks and referral certification and authorization.  
 
The 2024 final rule requires impacted payers to implement and maintain a PA application programming 
interface (API) to facilitate electronic PA of medical items and services. In the proposed rule, CMS 
includes proposals from the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology to adopt 
updated versions of certain health IT standards and specifications for interoperability APIs. Payers would 
be required to report API endpoints and API usage metrics to CMS to allow the agency to monitor the 
adoption and performance of electronic PA systems. Further, impacted payers would have to incorporate 
coverage and documentation requirements into their APIs to support the electronic PA of drugs covered 
under a medical benefit beginning Oct. 1, 2027. Adopting these updated versions would support federal 
alignment of interoperability and health information exchange standards. Ensuring sufficient provider 
participation in testing the standards is crucial to evaluate their viability and readiness for widespread 
implementation across payers and providers. Accordingly, we strongly urge CMS to conduct 
demonstrations and delay the implementation date. It is important that any solution be fully developed and 
tested prior to wide scale industry rollout and required usage. 
 
Public Reporting Requirements 
The LHA strongly supports the expansion of public PA metrics reporting to include drugs for the first time, 
including total number of requests, approval and denial rates, appeal outcomes, and average time to a 
decision. We believe that requiring plans to report on PA processes promotes much-needed transparency 
and the opportunity to build accountability. Plan PA metrics buried on individual plan sites add little to no 
benefit to patients. Instead, we believe it is important that CMS directly collect these data to 1) make them 
publicly available; and 2) use it to guide oversight and enforcement activities. Year-over-year comparisons 
could demonstrate positive or negative PA trends, which would be useful information for patients, 
providers, and payers. Further, we encourage CMS to create mechanisms whereby this data is used to 
guide oversight and enforcement activities. This would help ensure compliance with CMS rules, which 
have direct impacts on patient access to care and outcomes. To truly realize these benefits, oversight and 
enforcement by CMS will be key.  
 
We appreciate and support the administration’s efforts to reduce administrative burden and improve 
workflow automation, particularly when it comes to onerous PA requirements. If you have any questions or 
need additional information, please contact LHA VP of Healthcare Reimbursement Kevin Bridwell at 
kbridwell@lhaonline.org.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Paul A. Salles 
President & CEO

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Paul A. Salles, President & CEO, Louisiana Hospital Association (LHA).
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** LHA represents more than 150 hospitals and health systems in Louisiana.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

LHA supports extending CMS prior authorization interoperability requirements to drugs and to small-group FF-SHOP QHP issuers, emphasizing the burden of payer-specific workflows and the need for standardization. LHA also supports shorter decision timeframes, public PA metrics, and endpoint/usage transparency, but urges CMS to conduct demonstrations and delay implementation until standards are fully tested.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING; API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** HIPAA administrative simplification authority; no detailed CFR citations beyond the proposed rule reference.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR, Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD) IG, Prior Authorization Support (PAS) IG, MedicationRequest resource, HCPCS J-codes, APIs.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Extension of ePA standards to drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; FHIR-IG-REQUIRED
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** Variation in PA submission processes creates multiple workflows, administrative costs, reprocessing, appeals, and burnout. Existing CRD/PAS functionality can support medical benefit drugs.
- **Specific request:** Finalize requirements to extend standardized electronic PA and electronic data exchange reforms to drugs.

**Topic 2: Expansion of impacted payers, including FF-SHOP**
- **Provision ID:** FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** Including additional payer types increases standardization across plans and encourages provider adoption.
- **Specific request:** Finalize expansion to MA, Medicaid/CHIP FFS and managed care, QHPs, and FF-SHOP small-group QHPs.

**Topic 3: Shorter PA decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with stronger standards.
- **Rationale:** PA directly affects patient care and should be expedited when FHIR transactions provide required information electronically.
- **Specific request:** Apply 72-hour standard and 24-hour urgent timeframes across all medical services when FHIR technology is used, not just drugs.

**Topic 4: Updated interoperability standards and testing**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; ONC-STANDARDS-UPDATE
- **Position:** Support with modification.
- **Rationale:** Updated standards can support federal alignment, but implementation must be fully developed and tested with provider participation.
- **Specific request:** Conduct demonstrations and delay the implementation date until viability and readiness are validated.

**Topic 5: Public reporting and accountability**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Support.
- **Rationale:** PA metrics promote transparency and can guide oversight; plan-by-plan posting alone is not useful if buried on individual websites.
- **Specific request:** CMS should collect and publicly post PA metrics and use the data for oversight and enforcement.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S1/S18/S37:** Supports mandatory electronic PA standards for drugs but urges demonstrations and delayed implementation after testing.
- **S12/S15/S21:** Supports extending medical benefit drug PA into the FHIR framework and believes existing CRD/PAS resources support this, but asks for testing before rollout.
- **S20/S43:** Supports shorter PA timeframes and asks CMS to apply 72-hour/24-hour timeframes more broadly across medical services when FHIR is used.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Strongly supports PA metrics reporting, CMS collection, public availability, and oversight use.
- **S40-S42:** Supports adding small-group QHP issuers on FF-SHOP to the requirements.
- **S44-S56/S60-S65:** Supports updated interoperability standards and HIPAA alignment but requests demonstrations and a delayed implementation date.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize extension of electronic PA standards to drugs.
2. Finalize expansion of impacted payers to include FF-SHOP small-group QHPs.
3. Require 72-hour standard and 24-hour urgent responses for all medical services when FHIR transactions are used.
4. Conduct demonstrations and delay implementation until standards are fully tested with provider participation.
5. Require CMS-centralized collection and publication of PA metrics.
6. Use public PA metrics to guide oversight and enforcement.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Payer-specific workflow variation, provider burnout, patient delays, insufficient testing before implementation, metrics buried on plan websites.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Dangerous treatment delays, clinician burnout, waste, denials from inadvertent errors, administrative cost.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Multiple payer processes, differing medical vs drug PA workflows, provider testing/readiness, lack of centralized reporting.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** LHA represents more than 150 hospitals and health systems; no formal statistics beyond describing proposed decision timeframes.
- **Studies or research referenced:** None cited.
- **Examples provided:** PA variation across plans causing errors and appeals; medical benefit drugs using MedicationRequest and J-codes within CRD/PAS capability.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Hospitals, clinicians, staff, patients, payers, utilization review entities, QHP issuers, small group employers/enrollees.
- **Economic implications:** Standardization may reduce provider administrative costs and health system waste; testing/delay may prevent costly failed implementation.
- **Technical feasibility:** LHA views the technology as promising but requiring demonstrations and provider testing before broad mandatory use.
- **Patient care impact:** Faster PA decisions and standardized electronic workflows can reduce delays and interruptions in drug therapy.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive with implementation/testing modifications.
- **Tone:** Professional, provider-centered, supportive.
- **Priority level:** High.

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "The expansion of standardized electronic PA transactions for drugs has the potential to save patients, providers, and utilization review entities considerable time and resources" - Context: Support for extending ePA to drugs.
2. "The proposed timeframes remain too lenient." - Context: Request for faster decision standards.
3. "We strongly urge CMS to conduct demonstrations and delay the implementation date." - Context: Testing and readiness recommendation.
4. "Plan PA metrics buried on individual plan sites add little to no benefit to patients." - Context: Support for centralized reporting and oversight.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports delay for demonstrations/testing.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Major focus on provider workflows, burnout, and administrative burden.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - Calls for demonstrations and provider testing.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - Discusses CRD/PAS readiness and updated standards.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Emphasizes delays and treatment interruptions.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strong support for public metrics and CMS oversight.
- [x] **FF-SHOP-REQUIREMENTS** - Explicitly supports including small-group FF-SHOP issuers.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Highlights variation across payer PA protocols and drug/medical workflows.
